column1: #     SLIDES 1-5 STANDING, 18 Aug       191 wpm   <- 1140 words in 5:58
# The fourth is the best evidence yet: it is the current text, standing, across
# the Act 0/Act 1 boundary, including the two densest slides in the primer.
# Per-slide it ran 190 / 201 / 197 / 181 wpm — steady, and brisk.
# All four runs were SOLO. **The planning rate stays 140** (MB, 18 Aug: "we
# still need a comfortable margin for nervosity & interruptions of any kind, so
# don't take my WPM as the target"). 191 minus 22% is 149, so 140 is about six
# per cent more conservative than the measurement supports — which is the right
# WHAT THE MEASUREMENT VALIDATES, rather than loosens: slides 1-5 hold 1140
# words against 7:05 of caps. At 140 that is 8:09, i.e. +1:04 — exactly what
# `make timing` has been reporting. The tool is right and the overruns are real
# WHAT IT ALSO SAYS, and this is the part worth acting on: 191 wpm is fast for
# dense material delivered in a second language. The headroom a solo run creates
# is best spent slowing down, not on more words.
# A cap is the AIRTIME a slide gets on the night. It is a pacing decision and
# does NOT move when the planning rate moves — the rate only decides how many
# words fit inside it. Caps total 40:50 against a 45:00 slot.
# `demo` rows score at the lower DEMO_WPM — on a live edit you talk around
# typing and pause while the room reads the error. The four demos are 9:15,
# 20% of the slot, and before these rows existed the tool could not see one
# `stub` rows are v2 slides that do not exist yet, carrying their planned cap
# so `make timing` measures the deck we INTEND rather than the deck we have.
# ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH for durations. The plan quotes this file, never the
# reverse: three drafts running, hand-carried arithmetic in the plan drifted in
# the same direction every time (Part 8/C10, C12).
# These were `stub` rows until the act was written, and stayed `stub` after it
# was — so `make timing` printed the planned cap and hid the real script. They
# are `prose` now: the act measures long against its caps and the tool has to
# say so, which is the whole point of C10. Cut #5 (merge connectives and
# quantifiers) is the reserve if the read-through confirms it.
# ── Act 2 · Ground floor — 2:20 · all three exist ──────────────────────────
# a2-values and a2-promises are cues + a scripted landing line, so they carry
# an EST-WORDS declaration rather than a countable script (Part 6b/T).
